title: Parsing and C++ Streams - Title Slide
summary: Title slide introducing Unit 5g on Parsing and C++ Streams, taught by Mark Redekopp as part of CS103.
main_text: This unit covers parsing and C++ streams. The lecture is part of CS103 and is presented by Mark Redekopp. Topics include I/O streams, file streams, stringstreams, error checking, and strategies for choosing the right I/O approach.
notes_text: This is the introductory slide for Unit 5g. The unit builds on prior knowledge of cin/cout and extends it to file I/O and string parsing using C++ stream abstractions.

title: Recall: I/O Streams
summary: C++ uses streams as buffers for input/output, accessed through cin and cout objects from the iostream library, with OS-level stdin and stdout.
main_text: C++ and the OS use the notion of streams to temporarily store (aka buffer) data to be input or output and then uses the cin and cout objects (from the <iostream> library) to access those streams. The OS name for these streams are: stdin (keyboard) and stdout (the terminal). cin pulls data from stdin and cout places data in the stdout stream. When using cin >> x, the program reads from the input stream memory (stdin). When using cout << "text", the program writes to the output stream memory (stdout). The code example shows: #include<iostream> with int main() using std::cout << "It was the" << std::endl; and std::cout << "best of times."; for output, and std::cin >> x; for input.
notes_text: This is a review slide. The stream model is foundational to all subsequent topics in this unit. Understanding that cin and cout are objects that interface with OS-level stdin/stdout buffers is essential before moving to file streams and stringstreams.

images.description: Diagram showing the flow of data: keyboard connects to OS, which fills input stream memory (stdin) with characters like '7', '5', 'y'. cin reads from this buffer. A separate diagram shows cout writing to output stream memory (stdout) which the OS sends to the terminal display.

title: File Streams
summary: C++ uses ifstream and ofstream objects to read from and write to files, leveraging the same interface as cin and cout through the fstream library.
main_text: C++ leverages the SAME interface that cin and cout provide to: Read data IN from a file (like cin, but data comes from a file not the keyboard) and Write data OUT to a file (like cout, but data goes to a file not the terminal). The counterpart to cin is an ifstream object. The counterpart to cout is an ofstream object. To read from a file: #include <iostream>, #include <fstream>, using namespace std; then create ifstream ifile("dat1.txt"); and use ifile >> x; to read, followed by ifile.close();. To write to a file: create ofstream ofile("dat2.txt"); and use ofile << "Hi there" << std::endl; followed by ofile.close();. The ifstream reads from the file into input stream memory, while ofstream writes from output stream memory to the file.
notes_text: The key insight is that C++ designed file I/O to use the exact same operators (>> and <<) as console I/O. This is possible through inheritance in the stream class hierarchy. Students should always remember to close file streams after use.

images.description: Diagram showing ifstream reading from dat1.txt file through OS into input stream memory, paralleling cin. A separate diagram shows ofstream writing from output stream memory through OS to dat2.txt file, paralleling cout.

title: Question: Why Do Streams Share the Same Interface?
summary: Asks how cin and ifstream both support <<, getline(), and fail(), and how cout and ofstream both support >> and I/O manipulators.
main_text: How is it that we can use <<, getline(), fail(), etc. on ifstreams and cin equally well? The slide shows two parallel code examples: one using cin >> x; if(cin.fail()) {...} and another using ifstream ifile("dat1.txt"); ifile >> x; if(ifile.fail()) {...}. Similarly, how is it that we can use >> and I/O manipulators (setw, fixed, etc.) on ofstreams and cout equally well? Another pair of examples shows cout << "It was the" << std::endl; alongside ofstream ofile("dat2.txt"); ofile << "Hi there" << std::endl; ofile.close();. The answer is inheritance, as explained on the next slide.
notes_text: This motivational slide sets up the explanation of the C++ stream class hierarchy. The fact that the same operators work on different stream types is a direct consequence of object-oriented inheritance.

title: Relationship of Input and Output Streams
summary: Stream classes are related through inheritance: istream is the base for ifstream and iostream(cin), ostream is the base for ofstream and iostream(cout).
main_text: Because they are related through inheritance. Where are getline() and operator>> defined? In the base class, std::istream. The class hierarchy shows: std::istream is the parent class, with std::ifstream and std::iostream (cin) as child classes that inherit from it. Similarly, std::ostream is the parent class, with std::ofstream and std::iostream (cout) as child classes. The istream class defines member functions including: istream::getline, istream::get, istream::ignore, istream::operator>>, istream::peek, istream::putback, istream::read, istream::readsome, istream::seekg, istream::sync, istream::tellg, and istream::unget. Because ifstream inherits from istream, all these functions are available on ifstream objects as well.
notes_text: This is a concrete example of inheritance in practice. The stream hierarchy is a classic example of polymorphism in C++. Understanding this hierarchy explains why the same code patterns work across cin, ifstream, and stringstream objects.

images.description: Class hierarchy diagram showing std::istream at the top with arrows pointing up from std::ifstream and std::iostream(cin) below it. Separately, std::ostream at the top with arrows pointing up from std::ofstream and std::iostream(cout). A sidebar lists istream member functions.

title: Checking for Input Errors and the End of Input - Section Header
summary: Section divider introducing the topic of checking for input errors and detecting the end of input in C++ streams.
main_text: This section covers how to check for input errors and detect the end of input when reading from streams. Topics include the fail() function, EOF detection, status bits, and patterns for safe stream reading.
notes_text: This section is critical for writing robust C++ programs that read from files or user input. Failing to check for errors is one of the most common bugs in student code.

title: Input Stream Error Checking
summary: Use cin.fail() to check if input conversion failed. The istream maintains three status bits: fail, EOF, and bad.
main_text: We can check errors when cin receives unexpected data that cannot be converted to the given type. Use the function fail() member function (i.e. cin.fail()) which returns true if anything went wrong opening or reading data in from the file. Internally, the istream class maintains 3 status bits: Fail (Unable to read the desired data), EOF (Hit the end-of-file / end-of-stream), and Bad (Ignore this one. It is rarely used). Example code: int x; cout << "Enter an int: " << endl; cin >> x; // What if the user enters "abc"? if(cin.fail()) { cout << "Error: I said enter an int!"; cout << " Now I must exit!" << endl; return 1; } cout << "You did it! You entered an int"; cout << " with value: " << x << endl;. When "abc" is entered for an int, the stream buffer contains 'a','b','c','\n' and all three status bits (fail, eof, bad) are initially 0.
notes_text: The fail bit is the most commonly checked status bit. It is set when the stream cannot extract the requested data type. The bad bit indicates a serious I/O error (like a hardware failure) and is rarely relevant in student programs. Always check fail() after every read operation.

images.description: Diagram showing cin stream buffer containing characters 'a', 'b', 'c', '\n' with three status bit indicators below showing fail=0, eof=0, bad=0, representing the state when non-numeric input is entered for an int variable.

title: Understanding Input Streams
summary: Step-by-step trace of how cin processes the input "512 123" across two successive >> extractions, showing stream buffer state at each step.
main_text:
User enters value "512 123" at the prompt. The trace shows: Initially X=0, stdin is empty. After the user types, cin buffer contains '5','1','2',' ','1','2','3','
'. After cin >> x, X=512 and cin buffer has ' ','1','2','3','
' remaining. cin.fail() is false. Then int y=0; cout << "Enter y: "; cin >> y; reads from the remaining buffer. Y becomes 123, cin buffer has just '
' left. cin.fail() is false. The >> operator skips leading whitespace automatically, which is why the space before '1','2','3' is consumed. The status bits remain fail=0, eof=0, bad=0 throughout.
notes_text: This example demonstrates that cin buffers all input at once and subsequent >> operations read from the buffer without waiting for new user input. The automatic whitespace-skipping behavior of >> is important to understand.

images.description: Step-by-step trace diagram showing the variable values (X, Y), cin buffer contents, and status bits at each stage of processing the input '512 123'. Each row shows the state before and after each cin >> operation.

title: When Does It Fail
summary: Demonstrates how entering "23abc" causes the first cin >> x to succeed (reading 23) but the second cin >> y to fail because 'a' cannot be converted to int.
main_text:
User enters value "23abc" at 1st prompt, 2nd prompt fails. Trace: Initially X=0, cin is empty. After input, cin contains '2','3','a','b','c','
'. cin >> x reads 23 into X, stopping at 'a'. cin buffer now has 'a','b','c','
'. cin.fail() is false because 23 was successfully read. Status bits: fail=0, eof=0, bad=0. Then int y=0; cout << "Enter y: "; cin >> y; attempts to read from the remaining buffer 'a','b','c','
'. Since 'a' cannot be converted to an int, Y remains unchanged (??), cin buffer still has 'a','b','c','
', and cin.fail() is true. Status bits: fail=1, eof=0, bad=0. The key lesson is that >> reads as many valid characters as possible and stops at the first invalid character.
notes_text: This is a critical example showing partial parsing. The >> operator is greedy: it reads as many characters as form a valid value of the target type, then stops. If no characters can be read for the target type, fail is set. The leftover characters remain in the buffer and cause cascading failures.

images.description: Trace diagram showing cin buffer states and status bits as '23abc' is processed. After first extraction X=23 with fail=0. After second extraction attempt for int y, fail=1 because 'a' cannot convert to int.

title: Take Care Mixing >> and Getline
summary: Mixing >> and getline causes problems because >> leaves the newline in the buffer, which getline then reads immediately as an empty line.
main_text:
User enters: 23 then Hi :). After cin >> x, X=23 and cin buffer contains '
','H','i',' ',':',')',' ','
'. cin.fail() is false. Then char y[80]; cout << "Enter y: "; cin.getline(y, 80); attempts to read. But getline reads up to the next '
', which is the very first character in the buffer. So Y gets an empty string '\0', and cin buffer advances past that '
' to 'H','i',' ',':',')',' ','
'. cin.fail() is false. Warning: >> stopped before the '
' and so getline will read that '
' and stop. This means the actual text "Hi :)" is missed by the first getline call.
notes_text: This is one of the most common pitfalls in C++ I/O. When mixing >> and getline, the newline left by >> causes getline to return immediately with an empty string. Two solutions exist: using a dummy getline call or using cin >> ws before getline.

images.description: Step-by-step trace showing cin buffer contents as >> reads 23 and leaves '\n' in the buffer, then getline immediately consumes that '\n' and returns an empty string instead of reading 'Hi :)'.

title: Solution: Use 2 Getlines
summary: One solution to the >> and getline mixing problem is to call getline twice: the first consumes the leftover newline, the second reads the actual data.
main_text:
User enters: 23 then Hi :). After cin >> x, X=23 and cin buffer has '
','H','i',' ',':',')',' ','
'. cin.fail() is false. Then char y[80]; cout << "Enter y: "; cin.getline(y, 80); - the first getline reads up to the '
', giving Y an empty string '\0', and cin buffer now has 'H','i',' ',':',')',' ','
'. Then cin.getline(y, 80); is called again - the second getline reads 'H','i',' ',':',')' up to the next '
', giving Y = "Hi :)\0". cin buffer is now empty. cin.fail() is false. The 1st getline() gets the rest of what is on the line with 23, second gets the next line.
notes_text: While this solution works, it is somewhat fragile because you have to know that there is exactly one newline to consume. The std::ws approach shown on the next slide is generally preferred as it is more robust.

images.description: Trace diagram showing two getline calls after >>. The first getline reads the leftover newline (empty result), and the second getline reads the actual 'Hi :)' text.

metadata.topic: Fixing >> and Getline with Double Getline

title: Alternate Solution: Use std::ws
summary: Use std::ws manipulator to advance past whitespace (including newlines) before calling getline, providing a cleaner solution than double getline.
main_text:
Use std::ws to advance to the next NON-WHITESPACE character in the stream. User enters: 23 then Hi :). After cin >> x, X=23, cin buffer has '
',' ','H','i',' ',':',')',' ','
'. Then char y[80]; cout << "Enter y: "; cin >> ws; - Before cin >> ws, the buffer has '
' at the front. After cin >> ws, the whitespace (including the newline) is consumed and cin buffer now starts at 'H','i',' ',':',')',' ','
'. Then cin.getline(y, 80); reads 'H','i',' ',':',')' into Y. cin buffer is now empty. cin.fail() is false. This is the preferred approach because it cleanly handles any amount of whitespace between the >> extraction and the getline call.
notes_text: std::ws is an input manipulator that extracts and discards leading whitespace from the stream. This is the recommended solution when mixing >> and getline. It handles multiple newlines and spaces gracefully, unlike the double-getline approach.

images.description: Trace diagram showing cin >> ws consuming the newline character, then getline successfully reading 'Hi :)' from the cleaned buffer.

title: File Streams and the File Pointer
summary: The ifstream object tracks the current read position using an internal file pointer (fp/getp) that advances automatically as data is read.
main_text: Your ifstream object implicitly keeps track of where you are in the file using a "file pointer" or "get pointer" ("fp" or "getp"). It is an internal member of the ifstream object. As you read data, it advances the file pointer automatically. Just as a video player tracks the current location (cursor) to indicate what frame it will play next, the file pointer (fp) tracks the current location in the file where you will read from next. Example: ifstream with fp pointing to the start of file containing 'O','n','c','e',' ','u','p','o','n',' ','a','...'. After char c; ifile >> c; the fp advances past the first character read, now pointing to 'n'.
notes_text: The file pointer concept is analogous to a cursor or playback position. Students should understand that every read operation advances the file pointer, and this is how sequential reading works. The file pointer can also be manually repositioned using seekg().

images.description: Two diagrams showing an ifstream object with a file pointer (fp) indicator. The first shows fp at the start of 'Once upon a...'. The second shows fp advanced by one position after reading char c with ifile >> c. A video player progress bar analogy is shown above.

title: File Streams and EOF
summary: A special EOF character marks the end of a file. The EOF and fail bits are set only when you attempt to read PAST the EOF, not when you read up to it.
main_text: A special EOF (end-of-file) "character" indicates the end of a file. An EOF flag will be set when you READ PAST the EOF. But the fail bit will ALSO be set when the desired data could NOT be read. So, the fail bit will be set when the EOF bit is, so it is probably just easier to use fail(). Example trace: File contains '...','T','h','e',' ','E','n','d','!','EOF'. Initially fp points before 'T', with fail=0, eof=0, bad=0. After char c; ifile >> c; fp advances to read 'd' and '!', with fail=0, eof=0, bad=0. After another char c; ifile >> c; fp hits the EOF marker. Now fail=1, eof=1, bad=0. The key point is that reading the '!' character that sits right before EOF succeeds, but attempting to read again when only EOF remains causes both fail and eof to be set.
notes_text: A critical distinction: reaching EOF does not immediately set the fail bit. The fail bit is set on the NEXT attempted read after EOF. This is why checking fail() after each read is essential and why loop conditions must be structured correctly.

images.description: Three-stage diagram showing file contents with fp position and status bits. Stage 1: fp before 'T', bits all 0. Stage 2: fp at '!' after reading, bits all 0. Stage 3: fp past EOF, fail=1, eof=1, bad=0.

title: When Does It Fail (File Streams)
summary: For file streams and stringstreams, the stream does NOT fail until you read PAST the EOF. Reading something that stops ON or AT the EOF will not cause fail() to return true.
main_text:
For filestreams and stringstreams, the stream does NOT fail until you read PAST the EOF. Reading something that stops ON or AT the EOF will NOT cause fail() or eof() to return true. Example with string s; ifstream inf(argv[1]); and file text 'T','h','e',' ','e','n','d','.','
','EOF'. First inf >> buf; reads "The" into s, fp advances past 'e', fail=0, eof=0, bad=0. Second inf >> buf; reads "end." into s, fp advances to the '
' before EOF, fail=0, eof=0, bad=0. Third inf >> buf; tries to read but fp is at '
' followed by EOF. The >> operator skips whitespace and finds only EOF, so s still contains "end." (unchanged), and now fail=1, eof=1, bad=0.
notes_text: This slide reinforces the concept that EOF detection is lazy - it only triggers when you actually try to read and there is nothing left. This is why the common pattern while(!file.fail()) can produce a bogus duplicate last entry if not structured correctly.

images.description: Three-stage trace showing file pointer position and status bits as three successive >> operations read from a file containing 'The end.\n EOF'. The third read fails because only whitespace and EOF remain.

title: Pattern for File I/O or Streams
summary: The three-step pattern for safe stream reading: Try to read data, Check if you succeeded, and only Use the data if the read was successful.
main_text: Step 1: Try to read data (>> or getline). Step 2: Check if you succeeded or failed. Step 3: Only use the data read from step 1 if you succeeded. If you read from a stream and then blindly use the data you read without checking for failure, you will likely get one BOGUS data value at the end! This three-step process is the fundamental pattern for all stream I/O in C++. It applies to cin, ifstream, and stringstream equally.
notes_text: This is arguably the most important pattern in the entire unit. The 'Try, Check, Use' pattern prevents the common bug of processing garbage data after a failed read. Students should internalize this pattern and apply it to every stream reading loop they write.

title: Which Option Works?
summary: Compares two loop approaches for reading integers from a file into a vector: checking fail() in the while condition vs. checking fail() inside the loop with break.
main_text: Goal is to read all integers from the file into a vector. Which of these works? Option 1 (WRONG): while(!ifile.fail()){ ifile >> x; nums.push_back(x); } - This fails because it reads, then pushes back x without checking if the read succeeded. After the last valid read, one more iteration tries to read past EOF, fails, but still pushes the old x value. Option 2 (CORRECT): while(true){ ifile >> x; if(ifile.fail()) break; nums.push_back(x); } - This works because it tries to read, checks for failure, and only uses x if the read succeeded. The data.txt file contains '7 8 EOF'. Following the 3 Step Process: 1. Try, 2. Check, 3. Use.
notes_text: This is a direct application of the Try-Check-Use pattern. The incorrect version violates the pattern by using data before checking. The correct version follows the pattern exactly. Many students write the incorrect version and end up with a duplicate last element in their vector.

title: Getting the Order Right
summary: Demonstrates the correct vs incorrect approach to the Try-Check-Use pattern with cin, showing how failing to check before using leads to processing bad values.
main_text: Be sure you CHECK whether the input failed before you USE the result! Correct Approach: int x, sum = 0; cout << "Enter an int: " << endl; cin >> x; // Check if we successfully read an int while(!cin.fail()) { sum += x; cin >> x; // What if the user enters abc } cout << "sum = " << sum << endl;. This works because it reads first, checks, then uses the value, and reads again at the bottom of the loop. Incorrect Approach: int x, sum = 0; while(!cin.fail()) { cout << "Enter an int: " << endl; cin >> x; // What if the user enters abc sum += x; // May use BAD value } cout << "sum = " << sum << endl;. This is wrong because it uses x (sum += x) before checking whether the read was successful on the next loop iteration.
notes_text: The correct pattern reads once before the loop ('priming read'), then reads at the end of each iteration. This ensures every use of x has been preceded by a successful read check. The incorrect pattern adds x to sum before verifying the next read, leading to garbage in the sum.

title: A Tangent: Implicit Type Conversion
summary: C++ provides type-conversion operators that allow objects to be implicitly converted to other types like bool or int, enabling objects to be used in if/while conditions.
main_text: Would the following if condition make sense? if(x){ cout << "Not empty" << endl; } where x is a List object? No! If statements want Boolean variables, not objects. But C++ provides type-conversion operators via operator overloading. The syntax is operator <type>(). Example: class List { Item* head; public: operator bool() { return head != NULL; } operator int() { return size(); } }; Now List x; x.push_back(2); x.push_back(3); if(x){ // calls operator bool() } int sz = x; // calls operator int(). This allows the compiler to automatically convert a List to bool when used in a boolean context, or to int when assigned to an int variable.
notes_text: This tangent explains the mechanism that allows streams to be used in if/while conditions. The istream class defines operator bool() which returns true if the stream has no errors, enabling patterns like while(cin >> x) and if(getline(file, line)).

title: Try and Check All in One!
summary: The istream class has operator bool() enabling the idiom while(cin >> val) which tries to read and checks for success in a single expression.
main_text: The istream class inherits an operator bool() which returns true if the stream has NO errors (i.e. did NOT fail or hit the EOF). ios::operator bool() { return !fail() && ...; }. So we can combine the TRY and CHECK into a single if/while statement: if/while(cin >> val) { /* process val */ }. In this approach cin does two things: It TRIES to extract input into the variable 'val', and it CHECKS for error occurred and returns 'true' if it successfully got input, 'false' on an error. Example: #include <iostream> using namespace std; int main() { int val, sum = 0; cout << "Enter a sequence of integers"; cout << " or Ctrl-D (EOF) to quit: "; cout << endl; while(cin >> val){ sum += val; // we know val is good } cout << "Sum is " << sum << endl; return 0; }. This follows the 3 Step Process: 1. Try (checkmark), 2. Check (checkmark), 3. Use.
notes_text: This is the most elegant and idiomatic C++ pattern for reading from streams. The expression cin >> val both attempts the read and evaluates to a boolean indicating success. This pattern is widely used in professional C++ code and should become the default approach for students.

title: A More Compact Way
summary: Shows three approaches to reading file data into a vector, highlighting the compact while(ifile >> x) pattern as the best approach.
main_text: Three approaches are compared for reading integers from data.txt (containing '7 8 EOF') into a vector. Approach 1 (WRONG, marked with X): while(!ifile.fail()){ ifile >> x; nums.push_back(x); } - reads then uses without checking. Approach 2 (CORRECT): while(true){ ifile >> x; if(ifile.fail()) break; nums.push_back(x); } - explicit try-check-use. Approach 3 (BEST, most compact): int x; while(ifile >> x){ nums.push_back(x); } - combines try and check in the while condition. Calling >> on an input stream will essentially return a Boolean: true = success, false = failure. This is the most idiomatic and recommended pattern.
notes_text: The while(stream >> variable) pattern is the gold standard for reading from streams in C++. It is concise, correct, and handles EOF properly. Students should prefer this pattern over the more verbose alternatives.

title: Getline() for char* (C-Strings)
summary: The istream::getline member function reads a whole line into a C-string character array, reading up to bufsize-1 characters or a newline.
main_text: We can get a whole line of text (including spaces) with getline(). The prototype is: istream& istream::getline(char *buf, int bufsize); It reads through a newline OR a max of bufsize-1 characters and then adds the null character to the end of the given character array. But getline() uses char* (C-Strings) - what if we want to use C++ strings? Example code: #include <iostream> #include <fstream> using namespace std; int main() { char myline[100]; int i = 1; ifstream ifile("input.txt"); if(ifile.fail()){ return 1; } while(ifile.getline(myline, 100)){ cout << i++ << ": " << myline << endl; } ifile.close(); return 0; }. With input.txt containing 'The fox jumped over the log.' / 'The bear ate some honey.' / 'The CS student solved a hard problem.', the output is: 1: The fox jumped over the log. / 2: The bear ate some honey. / 3: The CS student solved a hard problem.
notes_text: This is the C-string version of getline, which is a member function of istream. It requires a pre-allocated character array and a buffer size. The C++ string version (global function) is generally preferred in modern code because it handles memory automatically.

title: Getline() for std::string (C++ strings)
summary: The global getline() function reads a line into a C++ string, taking an istream reference, string reference, and optional delimiter character.
main_text: C++ string library (#include <string>) defines a global function (not a member of istream) that can read a line of text into a C++ string. Prototype: istream& getline(istream &is, string &str, char delim='\n'); where is = any input stream (ifstream, cin, etc.), str = A C++ string that it will fill in with text, delim = A char to stop on (by default it is '\n') which is why it is called getline, and it returns the updated istream (the 'is' object you passed in as the 1st arg). Again, it is NOT a member function!!! Wrong usage: myfile.getline(myline); // doesn't work. Correct usage: getline(myfile, myline); Example: int line_no = 0; ifstream myfile(argv[1]); string myline; while(getline(myfile, myline)){ cout << "Line: " << myline << endl; }
notes_text: It is crucial to remember that the C++ string version of getline is a free (global) function, not a member function. Students frequently make the mistake of calling it as a member function. The optional delimiter parameter is powerful for parsing delimited data like CSV files.

title: Notes on Getline()
summary: Getline reads text up to the delimiter, strips the delimiter from the result, advances the stream past it, and can ONLY return text - not numeric types.
main_text:
Prototype: istream& getline(istream &is, string &str, char delim='
');. Operation: The text from the input stream will be read up through the first occurrence of 'delim' (defaults to '
') and placed into str. The delimiter will be stripped from the end of str. The input stream will be pointing at the first character AFTER 'delim'. getline can ONLY get text!! It CANNOT convert to numeric (int or double) types! Example: ifstream myfile(argv[1]); string myline; getline(myfile, myline, '.'); With file content 'Hello,
T. TrojanEOF': Before getline(), the file stream points to the start 'Hello,
'. After getline(myfile, myline, '.'), myline contains 'Hello
T' (everything up to the first '.'), and the stream now points to the space after the '.'. The delimiter '.' is consumed but not included in the result.
notes_text: The delimiter behavior is often misunderstood. The delimiter character itself is consumed from the stream but NOT placed into the output string. Also, getline reads across newlines if the delimiter is not '\n'. For numeric conversion, you must use >> on a stringstream after getline.

images.description: Before/after diagram showing file stream state. Before getline with '.' delimiter: stream points to start of 'Hello,\nT. Trojan'. After getline: myline contains 'Hello\nT' and stream points past the '.' delimiter.

title: Stringstreams - Section Header
summary: Section divider introducing the topic of stringstreams, which allow treating strings as streams for parsing and formatting.
main_text: This section introduces stringstreams, a C++ feature that allows treating string objects as streams. Stringstreams enable parsing strings into individual values, building strings from multiple values, and performing type conversions between strings and numeric types.
notes_text: Stringstreams are one of the most powerful tools for parsing in C++. They bridge the gap between text processing (getline) and typed data extraction (>>), enabling sophisticated parsing of formatted text data.

title: Introducing Stringstreams
summary: C++ has three stream categories: I/O streams (cin/cout), file streams (ifstream/ofstream from fstream), and stringstreams (from sstream).
main_text: I/O streams use the keyboard (cin) and terminal (cout). File streams have the contents of a file as the stream of data, using #include <fstream> and #include <iostream> with ifstream and ofstream objects. Stringstreams have the contents of a string as the stream of data, using #include <sstream> and #include <iostream> with stringstream objects. This creates a unified hierarchy: all three stream types share the same interface (>>, <<, getline, fail(), etc.) but differ in where the data comes from or goes to.
notes_text: This slide positions stringstreams within the broader stream hierarchy. The key insight is that a stringstream treats a string the same way an ifstream treats a file - as a source of characters to be parsed. This is why the same operators and functions work on all three.

title: StringStreams as Input (like ifstream)
summary: A stringstream can be used like an ifstream, treating a string's contents as the data source for >> extraction, just as ifstream treats a file.
main_text: An ifstream object just brings the text of a file into a stream. Then you can use getline() and >> to read in the text into variables. But if the stream is just text, why can't we do the same with a string. Side-by-side comparison: File approach uses #include <iostream>, #include <fstream>, ifstream ifile("dat1.txt"); ifile >> x;. Stringstream approach uses #include <iostream>, #include <sstream>, stringstream ss("75 yes"); ss >> x;. Both work identically because stringstream inherits the same interface. The input stream memory for both ifstream and stringstream contains characters like '7','5',' ','y','...' that >> can extract from.
notes_text: This parallel comparison makes the concept concrete. A stringstream initialized with a string is functionally equivalent to an ifstream opened on a file containing that same text. The extraction operations work identically on both.

images.description: Side-by-side diagrams comparing ifstream and stringstream. Left: ifstream reads from dat1.txt file through OS into input stream memory. Right: stringstream reads from a string directly into input stream memory. Both have the same characters in their buffers.

title: StringStreams as Output (like ofstream)
summary: A stringstream can be used like an ofstream for output, using << to build a string in memory instead of writing to a file.
main_text: An ofstream object just brings the text of a file into a stream. Then you can use << to produce text from variables. But if the stream is just text, why can't we do the same to produce a string. Side-by-side comparison: File approach uses #include <iostream>, #include <fstream>, ofstream ofile("dat2.txt"); ofile << "Hi there" << std::endl; ofile.close();. Stringstream approach uses #include <iostream>, #include <sstream>, stringstream ss; int x = 42; ss << "Hi there " << x << std::endl;. Both write to output stream memory. The ofstream then flushes through the OS to dat2.txt. The stringstream keeps the data in its internal string buffer, which can be retrieved with ss.str().
notes_text: Output stringstreams are useful for building formatted strings without the complexity of string concatenation. They are especially handy when you need to combine text and numbers into a single string, as the << operator handles type conversion automatically.

images.description: Side-by-side diagrams comparing ofstream and stringstream for output. Left: ofstream writes to output stream memory, then through OS to dat2.txt file. Right: stringstream writes to output stream memory which stays in memory as a string.

title: C++ String Stream
summary: The sstream library lets you treat C++ strings as streams for parsing, buffering output, and data type conversions, especially useful with getline().
main_text: If streams are just sequences of characters, aren't strings themselves like a stream? The <sstream> library lets you treat C++ string objects like they were streams. Why would you want to treat a string as a stream? Parse out (break up) the pieces of a string, buffer up output for later display, and perform data type conversions. Very useful in conjunction with string's getline(...). Stringstreams combine the flexibility of string manipulation with the type-conversion power of stream extraction/insertion operators.
notes_text: This slide summarizes the three main use cases for stringstreams. The combination of getline (to read a full line) and stringstream (to parse that line into typed values) is the most important parsing pattern in C++.

title: C++ Stringstream: Application 1 - Parsing
summary: Stringstreams can parse a string of many values into separate typed variables using the >> operator, with a get pointer (getp) tracking position.
main_text: Can parse (split) a string of many values into separate variables. Example: #include <sstream> using namespace std; int main() { stringstream ss; ss << "2.0 35 a"; double x; int y; char z; ss >> x >> y >> z; return 0; }. After execution: x = 2.0, y = 35, z = 'a'. The stringstream uses a get pointer (getp) that tracks where the next >> or getline will start extracting data. Initially getp points to EOF (empty stream). After ss << "2.0 35 a", getp points to the start of '2.0 35 a EOF'. After ss >> x >> y >> z, getp advances through each value, parsing 2.0 as double, 35 as int, and 'a' as char.
notes_text: The getp (get pointer) in a stringstream works exactly like the file pointer in an ifstream. Each extraction operation advances the pointer past the extracted data and any leading whitespace for the next extraction.

images.description: Three-stage diagram showing the stringstream's internal buffer and getp position. Stage 1: getp at EOF (empty). Stage 2: getp at start of '2.0 35 a EOF' after insertion. Stage 3: getp at end after extraction of x=2.0, y=35, z='a'.

title: C++ Stringstream: Application 2 - Building Strings
summary: Use the .str() member function to retrieve the contents of a stringstream as a string, providing an alternative to string concatenation with to_string().
main_text: Use the .str() member function to create a large string from many values (i.e. return a string with the contents of whatever is in the stream). Alternative is to use to_string and the string + operator: to_string(2.0) + " " + to_string(35) + " a";. Example: #include<sstream> using namespace std; int main() { stringstream ss; ss << 2.0 << " " << 35; ss << " " << 'a'; string s = ss.str(); return 0; }. After execution, s = "2.0 35 a". The stringstream's internal buffer contains '2','.','0',' ','3','5',' ','a','EOF'. The .str() method returns the entire contents as a std::string.
notes_text: The stringstream approach to building strings is often cleaner than concatenation, especially when mixing types. With concatenation you need to_string() for every numeric value, but with stringstream the << operator handles conversions automatically.

images.description: Diagram showing stringstream buffer containing '2.0 35 a EOF' with getp pointer, and the resulting string s containing '2.0 35 a' after calling ss.str().

title: C++ Stringstream: Application 3a - Number to String
summary: Stringstreams can convert numbers to strings by inserting a number with << and extracting as a string with >>, equivalent to to_string().
main_text: Can be used as an alternative to to_string(). Use << and >> to convert numbers into strings (i.e. 12345 => "12345"). Same result as to_string(12345). Example: #include<sstream> using namespace std; int main() { stringstream ss; int num = 12345; ss << num; string strNum; ss >> strNum; return 0; }. After execution, strNum = "12345". The process: num starts as int 12345. ss << num inserts '1','2','3','4','5' into the stringstream buffer. ss >> strNum extracts the characters as a string "12345". The getp pointer starts at EOF (empty), moves to the beginning of '12345 EOF' after insertion, then to the end after extraction.
notes_text: While to_string() is simpler for basic conversions, the stringstream approach offers more control through I/O manipulators like setw, setprecision, and fixed, making it useful for formatted number-to-string conversion.

images.description: Three-stage diagram showing getp position in stringstream. Stage 1: empty with getp at EOF. Stage 2: buffer contains '12345 EOF' with getp at start. Stage 3: getp at end after extracting strNum='12345'.

title: C++ Stringstream: Application 3b - String to Number
summary: Stringstreams can convert strings to numbers by inserting a string with << and extracting as a numeric type with >>, equivalent to stoi() or stod().
main_text: Can be used as an alternative to stoi() or stod(). Use << and >> to convert strings into numbers (i.e. "12345" => 12345). Same result as stoi("12345"). Example: #include<sstream> using namespace std; int main() { stringstream ss; string strNum = "12345"; ss << strNum; int num; ss >> num; return 0; }. After execution, num = 12345. The process: strNum starts as string "12345". ss << strNum inserts '1','2','3','4','5' into the stringstream buffer. ss >> num extracts and converts the characters to int 12345. The getp pointer starts at EOF (empty), moves to the beginning of '12345 EOF' after insertion, then to the end after extraction.
notes_text: The stringstream approach to string-to-number conversion is safer than atoi() (which has no error checking) and equivalent to stoi()/stod(). You can check ss.fail() after extraction to detect conversion errors, which makes it more robust.

images.description: Three-stage diagram showing getp position in stringstream. Stage 1: empty with getp at EOF. Stage 2: buffer contains '12345 EOF' with getp at start. Stage 3: getp at end after extracting num=12345.

title: C++ Stringstream Reuse
summary: When reusing a stringstream, you must call both clear() and str("") to reset it. Alternatively, just create a new stringstream object.
main_text: Beware of re-using the same stringstream object for multiple conversions. It can be weird. Make sure you clear it out between uses and re-init with an empty string. Or just make a new stringstream each time. Option 1 (Reuse): stringstream ss; //do something with ss; ss.clear(); ss.str(""); // now you can reuse ss. Option 2 (Use new stringstream): stringstream ss1; //do something with ss1; // Just declare another stream; stringstream ss2; // do something with ss2. Both approaches work. The clear() call resets the status bits (fail, eof, bad), and str("") replaces the internal string buffer with an empty string. Both must be called when reusing.
notes_text: Forgetting to call clear() is a common bug. If the previous use set the fail or eof bit, those bits persist and cause all subsequent operations to fail even after str("") replaces the buffer content. Always call clear() BEFORE str("") when reusing.

title: Exercise: Stringstream Extraction
summary: Exercise asking students to determine the values of text, num, and val after extracting from a stringstream initialized with "Hello 103 2.0".
main_text: What's in each variable after execution? Variables: text (string), num (int), val (double). Code: string text; int num; double val; stringstream ss("Hello 103 2.0"); ss >> text >> num >> val;. Students should trace through the extraction: ss >> text extracts "Hello" (stops at whitespace), ss >> num extracts 103 (converts to int), ss >> val extracts 2.0 (converts to double). After execution: text = "Hello", num = 103, val = 2.0.
notes_text: This exercise reinforces the concept that >> extracts whitespace-delimited tokens and converts them to the target variable's type. The stringstream handles mixed types seamlessly.

title: Exercises: Stringstream Practice
summary: Lists in-class exercises for practicing stringstreams: Stringstream_in, Stringstream_out, and Date parsing.
main_text: In class exercises to practice stringstream concepts: Stringstream_in (practice using stringstreams for input/extraction), Stringstream_out (practice using stringstreams for output/building strings), and Date (practice parsing date strings using stringstreams). These exercises help students apply the stringstream concepts covered in the lecture.
notes_text: These hands-on exercises are essential for solidifying understanding. The Date exercise likely involves parsing a date string like '01/15/2025' using getline with '/' as delimiter and stringstream for numeric conversion.

title: Exercises: Parsing Practice
summary: Lists additional in-class exercises for combining getline and stringstreams: wordcount-all, wordcount, and wordcount_parens.
main_text: Use the following in-class exercises to practice the prior material and illustrate the next few slides: wordcount-all (count all words in a file), wordcount (count words per line using getline and stringstream), and wordcount_parens (count words within parentheses using delimited getline). These exercises build on the getline + stringstream pattern for real-world parsing tasks.
notes_text: These exercises progressively increase in complexity. wordcount-all can use just >> in a loop. wordcount requires getline to track line boundaries plus stringstream to count words per line. wordcount_parens requires custom delimiters.

title: getline() and stringstreams
summary: Combining getline to read whole lines and stringstream with >> to parse individual words enables counting words per line, handling variable-length lines.
main_text: Imagine a file has a certain format where you know related data is on a single line of text but aren't sure how many data items will be on that line. Can we use >>? No it doesn't differentiate between different whitespace (i.e. a ' ' and a '\n' look the same to >> and it will skip over them). We can use getline() to get the whole line, then a stringstream with >> to parse out the pieces. Example code: int num_lines = 0; int total_words = 0; ifstream myfile(argv[1]); string myline; while(getline(myfile, myline)){ stringstream ss(myline); string word; while(ss >> word){ total_words++; } num_lines++; } double avg = (double) total_words / num_lines; cout << "Avg. words per line: "; cout << avg << endl;. With input file 'The fox jumped over the log. / The bear ate some honey. / The CS student solved a hard problem.', this counts words per line and computes the average.
notes_text: This is the most important parsing pattern in the unit. The outer loop reads lines with getline, and the inner loop uses a stringstream to parse each line into words with >>. This two-level approach handles variable-length lines correctly because getline respects line boundaries while >> handles word extraction.

title: Using Delimiters
summary: Use getline with custom delimiters to extract specific portions of text, then parse those portions with stringstream and >> to get individual words.
main_text: Imagine a file has a certain format where you know related data is on a single line of text but aren't sure how many data items will be on that line. Can we use >>? No it doesn't differentiate between different whitespace. We can use getline() to get the whole line, then a stringstream with >> to parse out the pieces. Text file contains: garbage stuff (words I care about) junk. Code: vector<string> mywords; ifstream myfile(argv[1]); string myline; getline(myfile, myline, '('); // gets "garbage stuff " and throws away '(' getline(myfile, myline, ')'); // gets "words I care about" and throws away ')' stringstream ss(myline); string word; while(ss >> word){ mywords.push_back(word); }. Result: mywords = ["words", "I", "care", "about"] at indices 0, 1, 2, 3. The delimiter parameter in getline allows extracting just the content between specific characters.
notes_text: This technique is powerful for parsing structured text formats. By using getline with different delimiters in sequence, you can navigate through formatted text to extract exactly the portions you need. This is a simpler alternative to regular expressions for basic parsing tasks.

title: I/O Decision Tree (1)
summary: Decision tree for choosing the right I/O approach: first determine data source (keyboard/file/string), then whether item count is known or arbitrary.
main_text: Where is my data? Three options: Keyboard (use iostream [cin]), File (use ifstream), or String (use stringstream). Next question: Do I know how many items to read? If Yes, n items: Use for(i=0;i<n;i++) loop. If No, arbitrary: Use while(cin >> temp) or while(getline(cin,temp)) to read until failure/EOF. This decision tree helps students systematically choose the right stream type and reading pattern based on their specific I/O requirements.
notes_text: This decision tree is a practical reference for students when approaching any I/O problem. The first decision (data source) determines which stream class to use. The second decision (known vs unknown count) determines the loop structure.

images.description: Flowchart decision tree. Top node: 'Where is my data?' branches to three options: Keyboard (iostream/cin), File (ifstream), String (stringstream). Below: 'Do I know how many items to read?' branches to 'Yes, n items: Use for loop' and 'No, arbitrary: Use while(cin >> temp) or while(getline(cin,temp))'.
labels: Do I know how many items to read?

title: getline or >> Decision Tree
summary: Decision tree for choosing between getline and >>: use >> for numeric types, getline for text delimited by newlines, and getline with delimiter for special characters.
main_text: What type of data? If Text: use getline or >>. getline ALWAYS returns text. If ints/doubles: Use >> because it converts text to the given type. For text data, is it delimited? If Yes at newlines: Use getline(). If No, stop on any whitespace: use >>. If Yes at special chars (';' or ','): Use getline with 3rd input parameter (delimiter parameter). This tree helps decide between getline and >> based on the data type and delimiter requirements.
notes_text: This is the second part of the I/O decision tree. The key insight is that >> handles numeric conversion automatically while getline always returns text. For text data, the delimiter type determines whether to use getline (for newline or custom delimiters) or >> (for whitespace-delimited tokens).

images.description: Flowchart decision tree. Top node: 'What type of data?' branches to 'Text (getline or >>)' and 'ints/doubles (Use >>)'. Under Text: 'Is it delimited?' branches to three options: 'Yes at newlines: Use getline()', 'No, stop on any whitespace: use >>', 'Yes at special chars: Use getline with 3rd parameter'.

title: Choosing an I/O Strategy
summary: Summary checklist for choosing an I/O strategy: consider delimiters, whether to break data into pieces, and whether the item count is known or variable.
main_text: Is my data delimited by particular characters? If yes, stop on newlines: Use getline(). If yes, stop on other character: Use getline() with optional 3rd character. If no: Use >> to skip all whitespaces and convert to a different data type (int, double, etc.). If 'yes' above, do I need to break data into smaller pieces (vs. just wanting one large string)? If yes: create a stringstream and extract using >>. If no: just keep the string returned by getline(). Is the number of items you need to read known as a constant or a variable read in earlier? If yes: Use a loop and extract (>>) values placing them in array or vector. If no: Loop while extraction doesn't fail placing them in vector. Remember: getline() ALWAYS gives text/string. To convert to other types it is easiest to use >>.
notes_text: This comprehensive checklist consolidates all the decision-making for I/O strategy into one reference. Students should use this as a quick guide when approaching any parsing problem in C++.

title: A Tangent: Implicit Type Conversion (Student Example)
summary: Demonstrates type-conversion operators with a Student class example, where operator bool() checks GPA and operator int() returns the student ID.
main_text: Would the following if condition make sense? if(x){ cout << "Hi" << endl; } where x is a List object? No! If statements want Boolean variables, not objects. But C++ provides type-conversion operators. The syntax is operator <type>(). Example with Student class: class Student { private: int id; double gpa; public: operator bool() { return gpa >= 2.0; } operator int() { return id; } };. Usage: Student s1; if(s1){ // calls operator bool() - checks if GPA >= 2.0 int x = s1; // calls operator int() - gets the student ID }. Also shown with List class: class List { Item* head; ... }; with operator bool() { return head != NULL; } and operator int() { return size(); }; so if(x) checks if list is non-empty and int sz = x; gets the list size.
notes_text: This slide revisits the implicit type conversion concept from slide 19 with a more relatable Student example. The Student's operator bool() returns whether the student is in good standing (GPA >= 2.0), and operator int() returns the student ID. This mechanism is what allows stream objects to be used in boolean contexts.
